analysis.one_liner: Expands Medicare-style health coverage to every lawful U.S. resident, funded by new payroll taxes.
analysis.headline: Introduced in April 2007 by Senator Edward Kennedy with zero cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have created a new Medicare for All program covering every lawful U.S. resident not already on Medicare, phased in over five years. Benefits would be at least as good as what members of Congress and federal employees receive, including prescription drugs, mental health parity, and reduced cost-sharing for low-income people. It would be financed by a new 1.7% tax on wages above $25,000, a 7% tax on employers, and a self-employment tax. Rather than eliminating private insurance, it would let private plans offer coverage under contract, similar to the federal employees' health system, and allow supplemental private coverage on top.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main winners would be the uninsured and underinsured: every lawful resident under 65 not already on Medicare would be entitled to a comprehensive benefit package, with enrollment automatic at birth, at immigration, or by application, and no one could be dropped for changing jobs or getting sick. Low-income enrollees would get reduced premiums and cost-sharing. Workers whose employers currently offer coverage would pay the new wage tax but could gain portable, guaranteed coverage; families with expensive private plans could come out ahead if the tax cost less than their premiums. People who like their private plans could keep them, since private plans could contract to offer coverage and anyone could buy supplemental insurance.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The uninsured and underinsured under age 65

how_it_helps.text: Every lawful U.S. resident not already on Medicare would be entitled to coverage, enrolled automatically at birth, at immigration, or by application, and unable to lose it for changing jobs or getting sick.

The benefit package would be at least as good as what federal employees get, including prescription drug coverage as comprehensive as the Blue Cross/Blue Shield standard federal plan, mental health benefits with parity, preventive services, and home and community-based care.
Low-income enrollees would get reduced cost-sharing no less protective than Medicaid rules, and families would pay a single family premium rather than per-person charges.

Enrollees could keep any doctor under the public program, or enroll in a private plan offered under contracts similar to the federal employees' system, and could buy supplemental coverage on top of it.
States would be barred from cutting their Medicaid eligibility or benefits below the levels in effect when the bill passed, protecting the existing safety net.

analysis.who_pays: Employees would pay a new 1.7% tax on wages above $25,000 (rising with inflation), employers would pay a 7% excise tax on every enrolled employee's wages, and self-employed people would pay both shares on income above the threshold. Economists generally expect employer payroll taxes to be passed back to workers over time through slower wage growth. Workers and employers would pay these taxes instead of, or alongside, current premiums; collectively bargained plans would keep operating until existing contracts expired, so some union members would pay both for a time.

drawbacks.text: The bill imposed a new 1.7% tax on wages above $25,000 for employees and a 7% excise tax on employers for every enrolled employee, plus a self-employment tax — a real cost on top of existing payroll taxes, and one economists would expect employers to pass partly back to workers through lower wages.
Coverage was not free: benefits under the program remained subject to Medicare-style premiums, deductibles, and coinsurance, with reductions only for low-income individuals.
The program phased in over five years — adults under 25 and over 55 first, everyone else only in year five — so many uninsured people would have waited years for coverage.
The bill grandfathered collectively bargained health plans until existing union contracts expired, so workers under those agreements would not have gained the new program immediately.

By contracting private plans and allowing supplemental private coverage, the bill preserved much of the private-insurance layer it was billed as replacing, leaving administrative duplication largely in place.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: On paper, the trade was straightforward: broad, guaranteed coverage — including dental-free mental health parity and protections for low-income enrollees — paid for by a shared payroll tax that most working families would likely find cheaper than private premiums. But the design carried real costs and soft spots. The employer tax could suppress wage growth, the benefit package kept deductibles and coinsurance rather than eliminating out-of-pocket costs, and the five-year phase-in delayed help for the people who needed it most. It also stopped short of single-payer: private insurers kept a permanent contracted role, which preserved much of the administrative overhead the bill claimed it would reduce. Weighing it honestly, the potential gains for uninsured and underinsured Americans were large, but the bill was never refined or scored, so its true cost and workability were untested.

outcome.mechanism: Senator Kennedy introduced it alone, the Senate Finance Committee never took it up, no cosponsors ever joined, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Edward Kennedy introduced the Medicare for All Act in the Senate on April 25, 2007.
That same day the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance — the committee with jurisdiction over taxes and health programs — and no further action was ever recorded.
Not a single senator signed on as a cosponsor over the nearly two years the bill was pending.

The bill as written was a public guarantee of coverage for all lawful residents, delivered through Medicare plus contracted private plans, financed by a 1.7% employee tax on wages over $25,000 and a 7% employer payroll tax.
With no committee action, the bill never reached the Senate floor and received no vote of any kind before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The health status quo held: private insurers kept their existing market, employers avoided the new 7% payroll tax, and the tens of millions of Americans then uninsured got nothing from this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The health-care status quo and its incumbents

for.name: Sen. Edward M. Kennedy
for.role: U.S. Senator from Massachusetts; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Medicare for All Act and was its sole sponsor for the entire Congress.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance (Chair Max Baucus, D-MT)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill after it was referred; it sat untouched for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no opponent ever acted on the record; the only visible support was the Democratic sponsor, who had zero cosponsors from either party.

industries.note: The bill stopped well short of single-payer: insurers would remain as contracted private plans under the program, similar to the federal employees' system, and supplemental private coverage would continue. Their core employer-sponsored market would shrink as the public program became the primary payor, but their role would be locked in permanently.

Every employer would owe a new 7% excise tax on wages for enrolled employees, replacing at least part of what they currently spend on health benefits. Employers generally opposed paying health costs through taxation, and their resistance was a major obstacle to any payroll-financed coverage expansion.

The bill guaranteed drug coverage as comprehensive as a standard federal employees' plan, creating a much larger insured customer base, but payments would follow a schedule set by the Secretary rather than negotiated prices — potentially pushing drug reimbursement down.

More insured patients means less uncompensated care, but the program would pay Medicare-set rates, which are typically lower than private insurance rates, and existing Medicare provider agreements would extend to the new enrollees.
